text:
alex: ran a quick nsys capture to triage a perf regression in batching + kvcache, but hot CUDA kernels are missing from the timeline when using sampling + osrt. any ideas?

tara: hmm. what exact nsys flags did you use? sampling windows can miss short-lived kernels, and osrt bracketing can shift traces if markers are on a different thread.

alex: used this one-liner: 

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --duration=25s --sample-window=500us --output=tmp_run
```

alex: timeline shows long gaps and then a big convolution kernel, but earlier small matmul kernels that should be frequent are absent.

tara: two things to try: increase sampling density (smaller sample-window) or switch to bracketed capture using nvtx spans so you don't accidentally sample warmup. also check whether kvcache warmup happens before your capture start.

sam: also ensure OSRT markers are emitted from the same CPU thread that touches the NVTX markers. we had a case where worker threads post NVTX but the RT thread posts OSRT and nsys slices them weirdly.

alex: how do you recommend bracketing? right now our app does a 3s warmup then starts the request stream. i want to only capture steady-state.

tara: use capture-range with start/end markers and a short prewarm window. Eg emit NVTX "capture:start" after warmup, and "capture:stop" after steady-state. nsys --capture-range=nvtx:start|nvtx:stop (or the equivalent CLI) will focus. if you're on older nsys, you can use --capture-range=pid and start the workload after the profiler hooks attach.

sam: if sampling still misses small kernels, run a short non-sampling (full trace) capture for a couple seconds to identify exact kernel names and durations, then tune sampling window. full traces are bigger but super helpful for kernel ID.

alex: got it. i worry about trace size but can do a 5s full trace. any quick command suggestions?

tara: for a focused full capture: 

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --duration=6s --output=full_short --sample=none
```

tara: then open in the GUI and note kernel durations and inter-arrival times. that tells you what a safe sample-window is (<= 1/3 of typical kernel duration).

sam: another trick: enable kernel module timestamps in the trace (cuda timeline) and also capture OSRT markers to correlate queuing vs execution. look for KV cache stalls right before those small matmuls — if the cache is cold they may be batched differently and not show up in the same pattern.

alex: ok i'll run a 6s full capture with nvtx brackets, then follow up. one more: any flags for reducing noise from background CUDA housekeeping (memcpy, driver stuff)?

tara: filter by process or cudaContext in the GUI or use CLI filters: --processes <pid> or post-process with nsys stats to filter events. also set --cuda-activity to none if you only want kernels, but we usually keep cuda activity on.

nsys-bot: capture started (pid=4321) output=full_short.qdrep

alex: thanks. running now. will paste results if weird.

tara: if you still see missing kernels after full trace, paste the kernel names + durations. might be a kernel fusion/selection change where runtime picked a different algorithm under quantization or batch size.

sam: and if you see KV cache evictions aligning with the gaps, instrument the runtime to emit NVTXs on kvcache::evict and kvcache::hit — that makes correlation trivial.

alex: good tip. adding NVTXs to hit/evict events now.

alex: (update) full_short shows many small kernels ~120-200us; sampling with 500us was definitely skipping them. re-ran with --sample-window=100us and osrt+nivtx brackets and the timeline now matches expected hotspots. will iterate. :thumbsup:

tara: awesome. thanks for the follow-up — sounds like a sampling cadence mismatch + bracketing issue.

sam: nice. file the capture alongside the perf regression ticket so we have the ground truth trace.

alex: added qdrep to the ticket and noted flags used. closing for now unless i see more anomalies.
